chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a woman who fell ill during the month of Ramadan and died in Shawwal, so she bequeathed to me that I make up the fasts on her behalf. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Was she cured from her illness?' I said: 'No, she died in it.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not make up the fasts on her behalf, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not make it obligatory upon her.' I said: 'But I desire to make up the fasts on her behalf, and she had bequeathed that to me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'How can you make up for something which Allah did not make obligatory upon her? So, if you desire to fast for yourself, then fast.'

key_terms.لَمْ يَجْعَلْهُ عَلَيْهَا: Did not make it obligatory upon her

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on making up missed fasts for a woman who died while still ill in Ramadan?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the distinction between obligatory and voluntary fasting by ruling that a woman who dies while still ill in Ramadan is exempt from qada, as the obligation was not fixed upon her. It highlights the Shia principle that one may fast voluntarily on behalf of the deceased even if not strictly required, reflecting the flexibility in devotional acts. This ruling underscores the theological view that divine obligations are contingent upon capacity and cure, rather than mere time passage.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ali Bin Al Hakam, from Muhammad Bin yahya, from Abu Baseer, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, said,

‘I asked him<sup>asws</sup> about a woman who fell sick during a Month of Ramazan, and she died in Shawwal. So she bequeathed to me that I make up for it on her behalf. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Was she cured from her illness?’ I said, ‘No. She died in it’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Do not make up for it on her behalf, for Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic did not Make it to be (Obligatory) upon her’. 
I said, ‘But I desire to make up for it on her behalf, and she had bequeathed it to me with that’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘How can you make up for something which Allah<sup>azwj</sup> did not Make it to be upon her? So, if you desire that you Fast for yourself, so Fast’.
en.sarwar: 8. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Muhammad ibn Yahya from abu Basir who has said the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a woman who became ill in the month of Ramadan and dies in the month of Shawwal. She asked me, in her will, to complete Qada’ (compensatory fast), on her behalf. He (the Imam) asked, ‘Did she get well from her illness?’ I replied, ‘No, she did not get well, but she died from that illness.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Do not complete Qada’ (compensatory fast) on her behalf; Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, has not made anything obligatory on her.’ I said, ‘I like to carry out on her behalf because she has asked in her will.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘How can you carry out on her behalf something that Allah has not placed on her? If you like to fast for yourself, you may do so.’”
